## Development

Tests run from this directory:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests -q
```

Three tiers gate themselves and each names why it is skipping: see
[`tools/battery/README.md`](tools/battery/README.md) for what each covers and
how to run the gated ones:

| tier | selector | needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unit + packaging | `-m "not gpu and not bigcard and not assets"` | nothing but Python |
| assets | `-m assets` | about 6.9 GiB of byte-pinned mesh/static/init/native-history files |
| big card | `-m bigcard` | a CUDA device clearing the measured x4 floor: about 21.7 GiB free (the measured 20,446 MiB peak plus that card's own margin, computed by `woof.hex.device_admission`; re-fitted at the merged tip 2026-08-26 and re-shaped 2026-08-27) |

`WOOF_HEX_NO_LOCAL_GPU=1` (or `GPUWM_NO_LOCAL_GPU=1`, honoured so a box
configured for the engine behaves the same) bans device contact outright.
chunks.title: Development

chunks.text:
# 1. What woof hex is

## For someone who has never run an atmospheric model

An atmospheric model is a program that takes a snapshot of the atmosphere
(temperature, wind, moisture, pressure, everywhere at once) and advances it
forward in time using the equations of fluid motion. Feed it this morning's
atmosphere and it computes this evening's. The snapshot it starts from is
called the **initial conditions**; the ground it stands on (terrain height,
land use, soil type) is called the **static** data; and the arrangement of
points where the atmosphere is represented is called the **mesh**.

woof hex's mesh is not a flat rectangle over one region. It is a sphere tiled
with hexagonal cells (the whole planet at once) and the cells do not all
have to be the same size. You can make them 100 km wide over the oceans and
25 km wide over the region you care about, in one seamless mesh with no nest
boundaries. That is what "global variable-resolution" means.

The unusual part is where it runs: **one consumer graphics card**. The entire
model state lives in GPU memory and every step of the integration is CUDA.
There is no cluster, no MPI job, no supercomputer allocation. A 12 GiB gaming
card integrates the published 40,962-cell global mesh; a 32 GiB card
integrates the 163,842-cell mesh whose fine band is about 25 km; a 10 GiB
card runs a six-hour full-physics limited-area forecast cut out of a
global case.
chunks.title: 1. What woof hex is

chunks.text:
## What it is, precisely

- **The dynamics** (the fluid-motion core) is a port of MPAS-Atmosphere
  v8.4.1, held **byte-identical** to the native model as its correctness
  anchor, and deterministic: two runs of the same case produce
  byte-for-byte identical output.
- **The physics** (radiation, clouds, rain, turbulence, land surface) is the
  WOOF engine's suite, reached through a pinned seam, so woof hex and the
  `woof` distribution share one physics implementation rather than two that
  drift.
- **The tooling** is a set of doors: `doctor` reports what your install can
  reach, `mesh-check` validates a mesh, `cull` cuts a limited-area case out
  of a global one, `init` builds initial conditions, `forecast` runs the
  model, `swath` decides where a fine grid goes, `cycle` follows weather
  across cycles, `render` turns model output into product images. Each door
  refuses bad input by name rather than producing a plausible wrong answer.

## What it can do

Measured, not promised (the README states each measurement):

- 24-hour global forecasts on one card, deterministic across dual runs.
- Full-physics limited-area forecasts cut out of a global case with the
  `cull` door and driven at their boundary: six hours, 1,080 of 1,080
  steps on an 11,020-cell cut, a 6,224 MiB footprint on a 10 GiB card.
- Weather followed across forecast cycles: `swath` places fine grids from
  a coarse run's own fields, `cycle` cuts, forces and integrates them,
  two real cycles ran back to back, both fine forecasts completing
  1,080 of 1,080 steps.
- Initial conditions built from a WPS intermediate file (GFS, ERA5, or
  whatever you drive with) without running any native Fortran tool; a
  native-built "capsule" is an explicit compatibility mode, not a
  requirement (chapter 5).
- Product PNGs rendered from history files entirely through the Rust
  renderer, filed by domain, product, and valid day (chapter 7).
- New meshes at resolutions you choose, with their static fields, generated
  by the engine's `woof mesh` door with no native toolchain (chapter 4).
- Checkpoint/restart with bitwise-identical continuation, proven in the
  full-physics proof harness (chapter 6).
chunks.title: What it is, precisely

chunks.text:
## What it cannot do, stated up front

- **It is not bit-identical to native MPAS-Atmosphere and cannot be**:
  native is single-precision CPU; this is CUDA. Beyond the expected
  chaos-shaped divergence there are **three measured, one-signed
  differences**: the declared divergences of chapter 3. Read them before
  trusting a number.
- **No multi-GPU.** Two-node execution is built and proven bitwise
  partition-invariant, but it is not part of this release.
- **Forecasting runs from the wheel.** Since 0.3.2 `woof hex forecast`
  needs no checkout of either project: its drivers ship in the package and
  the physics seam is the installed `woof`, named in every receipt by
  version and `RECORD` digest (chapter 6.1). `cycle run` still needs a
  woof hex checkout for its per-cycle contract deck (chapter 6.9).
- **No data fetching.** woof hex ships no meshes, no static files, no
  meteorological data, and has no download command for them. Chapter 2 states
  plainly where each asset comes from.
- **Not long-range.** The measured upper-level warm drift (chapter 3)
  disqualifies this version for multi-day stratospheric work; it is bounded
  and fine at 24 h.
- **A run can stop early.** When a step fails validation (for example a
  vertical-velocity spike past 200 m/s) the model refuses to publish the
  step and stops rather than writing output it does not trust. A refusal is
  designed behavior, not a crash (chapter 3).
chunks.title: What it cannot do, stated up front

chunks.text:
## What hardware it needs

| | |
| --- | --- |
| GPU | Any CUDA device for the doors. For forecasts, memory is set by mesh size *and* by the card, and the two do not combine into a line: the footprint is a per-card core, plus two physics column workspaces charged at `min(cells, tile)`, plus a per-cell term (chapter 4). Measured at the merged tip on an RTX 5090, 2026-08-26: the 40,962-cell global mesh peaked at **8,874 MiB** (fits a 12 GiB card); the 163,842-cell mesh peaked at **20,446 MiB** and admits at the measured floor (the prediction plus that card's own margin, about 21.7 GiB free at x4, computed by `woof.hex.device_admission`) so it remains in practice a 32 GiB-card configuration. The core is a property of the card, and the door reads the card at the moment of the decision. |
| CPU/RAM | Modest. The doors are I/O-bound; the model state lives on the device. |
| Disk | Meshes, initial conditions, and history files are hundreds of MB to a few GB each. The optional byte-pinned test assets are about 6.9 GiB. |
| OS | Linux or Windows. Python 3.11 or newer. |
| CUDA | A driver whose CUDA major you know: the install chooses a matching CuPy wheel (chapter 2). |

Chapter 4 turns the footprint model into a sizing method for any card.
chunks.title: What hardware it needs

chunks.text:
# 2. Quickstart

This chapter goes from nothing to rendered forecast products. Every command
in it was run, in this order, on a fresh install before it was printed here:
the door commands against the installed 0.2.0 wheel, the forecast against the
repository checkout, the GPU steps on an RTX 5070 Ti. Where output is shown
it is that run's output, except where a block is marked as a *form*: the
shape of a line rather than a captured one. The card transcripts in 2.6 come
from a second machine, a 10 GiB RTX 3080; their `ADMISSION` lines are
re-derived on the model the door decides with today, from that card's own
driver reading, because
the model the original run printed has since been retired (6.2).

The true shape of the journey: the wheel installs in one command; the
doors then need three estates the wheel cannot carry (a CUDA-matched CuPy,
the Rust engines, the mesh assets), and `woof hex doctor` walks you through
closing each one by name.

## 2.1 Install

```sh
pip install recast-woof
```

That installs the Python package, its dependencies (numpy, netCDF4, scipy)
and the `woof` engine distribution (`woof>=2.8.0,<2.9`).

**No engine constraint of your own is needed.** The port and the engine are
one project and, in WOOF, one distribution, so the engine you install is the
engine the port runs. Through 0.3.1 the port pinned sixteen engine files by
SHA-256 and admitted one exact published engine; that pin retired when the
two moved together. The forecast now records the digests of those sixteen
files, the engine's version and, for a git clone, its commit in every
receipt. `woof hex doctor` reports the installed engine and whether it
carries every seam file; on a conforming install it reads `woof 2.8.0: all
16 seam files are in this install; the forecast records their digests`.

Then add the CUDA lane:

```sh
pip install "recast-woof[gpu-cu13]"
```

**There is one right answer here and it is CUDA 13.** Every GPU door in this
port goes through `require_cuda`, which refuses a CUDA runtime below `13000`
by name, so `cupy-cuda13x` is the only wheel the port can execute on. The
`[gpu-cu12]` extra still resolves (it is in 0.1.0's published metadata) and
a CuPy installed through it imports, allocates, runs cuBLAS and compiles an
NVRTC kernel, and is then refused at forecast launch with
`CudaRefusal: cuda.runtime_version=12090 < required 13000`. Do not use it.

Check the driver, because a CUDA-13 wheel needs a driver that serves CUDA 13:

```sh
nvidia-smi        # the CUDA version in the header is your driver's major
```

(On recent drivers that header field is spelled `CUDA UMD Version`, driver
610.74 reads `CUDA UMD Version: 13.3`. A driver below 13 cannot open this
port's CUDA lane at all, and no pip command changes that; `woof hex doctor`
reads the driver itself and says so rather than offering an install that
cannot work.)

Confirm what landed:

```sh
woof hex version
```

```json
{
  "distribution": "woof hex",
  "package": ".../site-packages/hexcore",
  "source_checkout": null,
  "version": "0.2.0"
}
```

Note `"package": .../hexcore`, the import namespace is `woof.hex`, not
`gpuwm_hex`. It was renamed from `mpas_port` at 0.2.0 (README, "The import
namespace"); everything you *type* is `woof hex`.
chunks.title: 2. Quickstart

chunks.text:
## 2.2 Doctor first

```sh
woof hex doctor
```

On a fresh install with the CUDA extra, the report looks like this:

```
INFO    distribution: woof hex 0.2.0
INFO    interpreter: Python 3.14.4 on Linux x86_64
OK      numpy (arrays; 48 modules import it at line one): imported, 2.5.2
OK      netCDF4 (reads and writes every mesh, static and history file): imported, 1.7.4
OK      scipy (the regridder's spatial index): imported, 1.18.1
PRESENT woof (the physics seam): woof 2.5.2 is installed
INFO    woof git checkout (the forecast lane only): ...
OK      cupy (the CUDA lane): imported, 14.2.0
INFO    woof fetch-bridges coverage: the woof installed here bundles no rw_mpas_convert, rw_mpas_init, ...
MISSING rw_mpas_init (the initial-condition builder): not found on any rung. ...
          cargo build --release --locked --offline -p rw-mpas --bin rw_mpas_init
MISSING rw_mpas_convert (the history converter): not found on any rung. ...
          cargo build --release --locked --offline -p rw-mpas --bin rw_mpas_convert
OK      rw_wrfbatch (the product renderer): found via woof's bridge directories: ~/.woof/bridges/rw_wrfbatch
INFO    mesh grid + static pair: external assets. ...

2 required item(s) missing: rw_mpas_init, rw_mpas_convert.
Run `woof hex doctor --explain` for the full remedy for each.
```

Doctor exits 1 while any required item is missing, so it works as a gate in
a script. `woof hex doctor --explain` prints the whole pasteable remedy
block for each finding; `woof hex doctor --json` emits the same findings as
data. Run doctor after every step below until it says `Every check passed.`
chunks.title: 2.2 Doctor first

chunks.text:
## 2.3 Close the gaps doctor names

### The Rust engines

The doors are orchestration only, all field data is handled by Rust
binaries built from the `woof` source tree. Two roads:

**The staged road.** `woof` publishes prebuilt bundles:

```sh
woof fetch-bridges
```

This stages verified binaries into `~/.woof/bridges`, which woof hex reads
directly (the run that produced the transcript above staged 59 files, every
one verified against its packaged pin). What it can supply depends on the
woof you have: the transcript above was taken against the published woof
2.5.2 wheel, whose bundle carries `rw_wrfbatch` and **not** `rw_mpas_init`
or `rw_mpas_convert`, which is exactly the shortfall the doctor reports
there. The four MPAS bridge binaries enter the bundle at woof 2.5.3, and
this distribution's declared range is `woof>=2.8.0,<2.9` (far past
2.5.3): a conforming install cannot
land on the engine that transcript was taken from. Doctor
asks the woof you actually have what its bundle declares, so it never sends
you to a staging command that cannot deliver the file.

**The build road.** From a `woof` source checkout, at `tools/rustwx`:

```sh
cd <gpuwm-checkout>/tools/rustwx
cargo build --release --offline --locked -p rw-mpas       # rw_mpas_init, rw_mpas_convert, rw_mpas_mesh, rw_mpas_static
cargo build --release --offline --locked -p rw-wrfbatch   # rw_wrfbatch
```

(Both commands were run for this manual; they finished in 36 s and 34 s on a
warm target directory.) Then point the doors at what you built:

```sh
export WOOF_HEX_RW_MPAS_INIT=<gpuwm-checkout>/tools/rustwx/target/release/rw_mpas_init
export WOOF_HEX_RW_MPAS_CONVERT=<gpuwm-checkout>/tools/rustwx/target/release/rw_mpas_convert
export WOOF_HEX_RW_WRFBATCH=<gpuwm-checkout>/tools/rustwx/target/release/rw_wrfbatch
```

A flag or environment variable naming a missing file is a hard error, never
a silent fall-through to the next rung of the search ladder (chapter 9 has
the full ladder). When everything is closed:

```sh
woof hex doctor
```

```
...
OK      rw_mpas_init (the initial-condition builder): found via $WOOF_HEX_RW_MPAS_INIT: .../rw_mpas_init
OK      rw_mpas_convert (the history converter): found via $WOOF_HEX_RW_MPAS_CONVERT: .../rw_mpas_convert
OK      rw_wrfbatch (the product renderer): found via woof's bridge directories: ~/.woof/bridges/rw_wrfbatch
...
Every check passed.
```
chunks.title: 2.3 Close the gaps doctor names

chunks.text:
## 2.4 Obtain the assets, stated plainly

**There is no fetch path in woof hex for any of these.** No
`woof hex fetch` command exists. If a document ever implies otherwise, it
is wrong. You need four things:

1. **A mesh grid file** (`x1.40962.grid.nc`, `x4.163842.grid.nc`, …), from
   the MPAS-Atmosphere project's published mesh downloads, from the
   `MPAS-Tools` generator, or from the engine's own `woof mesh` door
   (chapter 4). This quickstart uses the published 40,962-cell global mesh
   `x1.40962`: the one a 10 GiB card holds.
2. **The matching static file** (`x1.40962.static.nc`), carrying terrain,
   land use, soil and vegetation for that exact mesh. The published meshes
   have published statics; a generated mesh gets its static from the same
   `woof mesh` run. Grid and static must be the same mesh: the doors
   cross-check and refuse a mismatched pair by name.
3. **For the init door: a vertical-grid declaration.** The normal path is
   a `--vertical-spec` JSON (`gpuwm-hex.vertical-spec/v1`), from which the
   door constructs the vertical grid itself: no native toolchain anywhere
   in the loop. The compatibility mode reads the vertical out of a
   native-minted init-class file (`--capsule`); chapter 5 explains both
   and when to prefer which.

   **The example specs are not in the wheel.** They live at
   `components/hex/verification/vertical-specs/` in the repository, and
   `pip install` places a wheel, so the path 2.5 prints
   below does not exist on a fresh install: the door refuses with the
   absolute path it could not find, which is correct and is not a hint about
   where to get one. Take them from the repository and put them where
   2.5 expects.
4. **Meteorological input**: a WPS intermediate file from `ungrib` (GFS,
   ERA5, whatever you drive with), valid at your start time.

For 1 and 2, on this mesh, the public download and the registered row are the
same bytes: verified 2026-08-24 by fetching both archives fresh and hashing
what came out:

| file | from | bytes | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `x1.40962.grid.nc` | `x1.40962.tar.gz` | 56,039,332 | `9a9e1909a755dac209462ceb0bfffd77ac1b37503169568b7f296707ee612bb9` |
| `x1.40962.static.nc` | `x1.40962_static.tar.gz` | 94,766,584 | `cf1a47d4168327f06a8403555d6ed8b2fe1aff7f8b916bb7f6a754c34a10ac82` |

Both match `src/hexcore/drivers/mpas_mesh_binding.py` exactly, so the forecast door's byte
check passes on what the published downloads give you. That is a fact about
those archives, not a fetch path: woof hex still fetches nothing.

Sanity-check the mesh pair before anything expensive touches it:

```sh
woof hex mesh-check --grid assets/x1.40962.grid.nc --static assets/x1.40962.static.nc
```

```json
{
  "connectivity_indexing": "zero-based with -1 padding",
  "dimensions": { "maxEdges": 10, "nCells": 40962, "nEdges": 122880, "nVertices": 81920 },
  "grid": ".../assets/x1.40962.grid.nc",
  "grid_sha256": "9a9e1909a755dac209462ceb0bfffd77ac1b37503169568b7f296707ee612bb9",
  "passed": true,
  "static": ".../assets/x1.40962.static.nc",
  "static_sha256": "cf1a47d4168327f06a8403555d6ed8b2fe1aff7f8b916bb7f6a754c34a10ac82"
}
```
chunks.title: 2.4 Obtain the assets, stated plainly

chunks.text:
## 2.5 First initial conditions

Build an init from your WPS intermediate file. Every physics switch is
required and has no default, each one changes the numbers in a file that
would open cleanly either way, so a default would be a silent wrong answer.
Each refusal prints the native namelist key it corresponds to (chapter 5
maps them all).

```sh
woof hex init \
  --met     <path-to-WPS-intermediate> \
  --grid    assets/x1.40962.grid.nc \
  --static  assets/x1.40962.static.nc \
  --vertical-spec verification/vertical-specs/tc55-v1.json \
  --out     work/x1.40962.init.nc \
  --start-time 2026-08-12_06:00:00 \
  --nfglevels 34 --nfgsoillevels 4 \
  --extrap-airtemp lapse-rate --use-spechumd no \
  --theta-adv-order 3 --coef-3rd-order 0.25 \
  --virtual-factor reproduce-fortran \
  --deep-soil-moisture reproduce-fortran \
  --landuse-table MODIFIED_IGBP_MODIS_NOAH \
  --frac-seaice yes --tsk-seaice-threshold 100.0 \
  --oned-underflow preserve
```

This is the native-free mint: `--vertical-spec` names a versioned JSON
vertical declaration and no native artifact appears anywhere in the
lineage (the receipt records `native_runtime_dependency: false`). The
compatibility mode passes `--capsule` + `--reference` naming a
native-minted init-class file instead; chapter 5.1 has both modes and
their receipts. `--nfglevels` must cover the levels actually in your met
file; declare too few and the door refuses with the real count (the
proving run's met file, a GFS intermediate, carried 34). The run above
wrote a 385 MB `x1.40962.init.nc` plus
`x1.40962.init.nc.provenance.json`: the SHA-256 of every input, the
engine binary, the argv, the engine's own receipt, and the output. The
engine step takes about 2 s; the first mint for a mesh spends minutes in
the door's geometry solve, and the keyed cache brings a re-mint down to
about a minute.
chunks.title: 2.5 First initial conditions

chunks.text:
## 2.6 Ask the card first

The forecast lane is the one step whose answer depends on your hardware, so
ask before you spend anything on it. It runs on what you installed: the
drivers ship in the wheel and the physics seam is the installed `woof`
(2.1), so no checkout of either project is needed.

```sh
woof hex forecast --preflight \
  --mesh    x1.40962 \
  --grid    assets/x1.40962.grid.nc \
  --static  assets/x1.40962.static.nc \
  --init    work/x1.40962.init.nc \
  --init-source "GFS 2026-08-12 06Z" \
  --hours 1.0 --history-every-minutes 30 \
  --out work/fc-01
```

Through 0.3.1 this command also needed `--repo <gpuwm-hex-checkout>/tree`
(the drivers were not in the wheel) and `--gpuwm-checkout` (a woof git
clone, only so receipts could name a commit). Both flags are still
accepted: `--repo` is reported and ignored, and a clone passed as
`--gpuwm-checkout` is recorded by commit instead of by the install's
version and `RECORD` digest.

On a card that holds the mesh, preflight binds it, admits it, runs the
driver's own source-pin and host checks, and exits 0. This transcript is
from a 10 GiB RTX 3080 with a desktop session on it, run 2026-08-25; the `ADMISSION` and
`ARCHITECTURE` lines are the ones the door prints for that card and that
free reading today:

```
[mesh-binding] bound x1.40962: nCells=40962, nEdges=122880, dx=120000.0 m, dt=120.0 s
BIND mesh=x1.40962 rebound=True dt=120.0 s
ADMISSION mesh=x1.40962 cells=40,962 card=68 SM row=measured global predicted=5,682.0 MiB margin=884.0 MiB free=9,097.0 MiB of 10,239.5 MiB -> admitted
ARCHITECTURE sm=sm_86 -> admitted, anchored: the 2026-08-25 anchor (evidence/sm86-tier-20260825/RECEIPT.md, evidence pin 75437c663c9894dc...)
PREFLIGHT mesh=x1.40962 problems=0 status=preflight_passed
```

The card is read at the moment of the decision (`card=68 SM`, and the row
selected for it) so a 10 GiB desktop is priced as itself. On this free
reading it admits `x1.40962`, `v15.150.38857` and `u96.64002`; the refusals
earlier releases printed for those three were a 32 GiB card's arithmetic
quoted at a 10 GiB part, and 6.2 has the whole story.

On a request the card really does not hold, it says so with numbers. The
same card and the same free reading, asked for the 163,842-cell
`x4.163842`:

```
ADMISSION mesh=x4.163842 cells=163,842 card=68 SM row=measured global predicted=17,000.2 MiB margin=884.0 MiB free=9,097.0 MiB of 10,239.5 MiB -> REFUSED
PREFLIGHT REFUSED device memory admission refused --mesh x4.163842: the fitted
footprint for 163,842 cells is 17,000.2 MiB and the decision holds back 884.0
MiB, so it needs 17,884.2 MiB free; this device reports 9,097.0 MiB free of
10,239.5 MiB, short by 8,787.2 MiB. ... This card fits the registered mesh(es)
conus-x1.2971, r4.75.11020, ... u96.64002, v15.150.38857, x1.40962 at this
moment (68,440 cells fit); re-run --mesh with one of them, or free the memory
the shortfall names and re-run.
```

Preflight exits 1 on a refusal and touches no CUDA beyond the memory and
device-properties queries; a missing input is *reported* alongside the card
verdict rather than hiding it. Chapter 6.2 explains the model it decides
with.
chunks.title: 2.6 Ask the card first (1)

chunks.text:
What the run checks before CUDA is touched, stated here rather than
discovered mid-launch: the sixteen `woof` seam files are hashed and
recorded, and a missing one is refused by name; the drivers verify their own
executing modules by SHA-256 against their pins.
Both read the installed copies, which are the copies that execute.
chunks.title: 2.6 Ask the card first (2)

chunks.text:
## 2.7 First forecast

Same command without `--preflight`:

```sh
woof hex forecast \
  --mesh    x1.40962 \
  --grid    assets/x1.40962.grid.nc \
  --static  assets/x1.40962.static.nc \
  --init    work/x1.40962.init.nc \
  --init-source "GFS 2026-08-12 06Z" \
  --start-time 2026-08-12_06:00:00 \
  --hours 1.0 --history-every-minutes 30 \
  --out work/fc-01 \
  --case-label quickstart
```

The same integration, from the init built in 2.5, took **97.8 s of
integration and 146 s wall on a 16 GiB RTX 5070 Ti**: 1 hour, 30 steps at
dt = 120 s, full physics, three history files, exit 0. That measurement was
taken through `tools/run_cuda_v841_forecast_mesh.py`, the driver this door
now drives; the door adds the admission decision in front of it and the
receipt and render command behind it, and changes nothing in between.

Re-run on 2026-08-27 on the 10 GiB RTX 3080 in a desktop, from the installed
wheel and a published `woof` 2.5.6 clone: **165.4 s of integration and 244 s
wall**, same 30/30 steps, same three frames, `status=passed`.

When it finishes, `--out` holds three history files (analysis, +30 min,
+60 min), `cuda-v841-forecast-receipt.json` (the driver's receipt, stating
exactly what this run claims and, at equal prominence, what it does not)
and `forecast-receipt.json`, the door's own, carrying the admission
decision, the mesh binding, the driver's receipt embedded whole, and the
render command. The door's last two lines have the form:

```
DOOR mesh=<row> steps=<n> frames=<n> status=passed out=<out>
NEXT woof hex render --history <out>/cuda-history.<valid-time>.nc --mesh <grid> --out <out>/png --simulation-start <start>
```
chunks.title: 2.7 First forecast

chunks.text:
## 2.8 First rendered products

Spell it out, and add `--window focus`, which the `NEXT` line does not
carry. The door's default window is `mesh`, and the `rw_mpas_convert` in
every published bundle answers `unknown render window 'mesh' (known: focus,
global)`, so the pasted `NEXT` line fails on a published engine (7.1).
`render` needs no checkout and no GPU:

```sh
woof hex render \
  --history work/fc-01/cuda-history.2026-08-12_07.00.00.nc \
  --mesh    assets/x1.40962.grid.nc \
  --out     work/png \
  --simulation-start 2026-08-12_06:00:00 \
  --window  focus \
  --products all
```

```
CONVERT CONVERTED  .../frames/wrfout_d01_2026-08-12_07_00_00  0.053s  107377492 bytes  35 written  3 absent
FRAME 2026-08-12T07:00:00 rendered=41 skipped=0 failed=0
MANIFEST work/png/render-manifest.json
SCRATCH cleared work/png.render-scratch
DOOR rendered=41 skipped=0 failed=0 out=work/png
```

41 product PNGs, filed under `work/png/<domain>/<product>/<valid-day>/`
(for this mesh the focus window is `d01-22km`), with a
`render-manifest.json` carrying engine digests, per-frame results, and the
exact invocations. 3.6 seconds on the proving node. That is the whole loop:
install → doctor → assets → init → forecast → pictures.

Re-run 2026-08-27 on a desktop against the published 2.5.7 bridge bundle:
**49 rendered, 0 skipped, 0 failed, 7 s**, same `d01-22km` tree. The count
moved because the renderer's catalog grew, not because anything here changed.
End to end (empty machine to these pictures, including every command that
failed on the way) **16 min 46 s**, with the mesh pair and the met file
already on disk.
chunks.title: 2.8 First rendered products

chunks.text:
## Where to next

- Something refused? Chapter 8 indexes the refusals you will actually meet.
- Want your own mesh, or to know what fits your card? Chapter 4.
- Want to understand what you just ran before trusting it? Chapter 3.
chunks.title: Where to next

chunks.text:
# 3. Concepts

Five ideas carry the whole product. This chapter states each one plainly.

## 3.1 Mesh, static, init

A run stands on three files, and they must agree with each other:

- **The mesh** (`*.grid.nc`) is the geometry: the centers, edges and
  vertices of the hexagonal cells tiling the sphere, and the connectivity
  between them. It says *where* the atmosphere is represented and how finely,
  and nothing about what the ground or the air is like.
- **The static** (`*.static.nc`) is the ground: terrain height, land use,
  soil category, vegetation fraction, gravity-wave-drag roughness, physical
  facts interpolated onto that exact mesh. A static built for one mesh is
  meaningless on another, which is why every door cross-checks the pair and
  refuses a mismatch by name.
- **The init** (initial conditions) is the atmosphere at the start moment:
  temperature, wind, moisture, pressure and soil state on that mesh at one
  valid time, interpolated from a meteorological source (GFS, ERA5, …) plus
  the vertical grid the model integrates on.

The mesh and static are reusable for years; the init is per-forecast.
chunks.title: 3. Concepts

chunks.text:
## 3.2 The doors

A *door* is a command a user can walk through: it validates its inputs,
names any refusal, does its work through proven engines, and writes a
receipt. The 0.2.0 doors were `woof hex version`, `doctor`, `mesh-check`,
`oracle-gate`, `cull`, `init`, `forecast`, `swath`, `cycle` and `render`,
and 0.3 added `mesh-plan`, `intermediate`, `lbc` and `pair`; chapter 9.1 tabulates what each one needs, and `cycle` has its own
document ([`docs/cycle-door.md`](../cycle-door.md)). The engine side
contributes `woof mesh` (mesh + static generation) and
`woof fetch-bridges` (engine staging).

**Forecasting is a door, and it runs from the wheel.**
`woof hex forecast` runs the model, and `cycle run` drives it. Its drivers
ship in the package and verify their own executing modules by SHA-256 before
CUDA is touched; the physics seam is the installed `woof`, whose version and
`RECORD` digest go into every receipt so the executed seam source can be
named. A `woof` git clone passed as `--gpuwm-checkout` is named by commit
instead (chapter 6.1).

**Fetching is deliberately not a door.** Nothing in woof hex downloads
meshes, statics, or meteorological data.

The doors' data paths are Rust (`rw_mpas_init`, `rw_mpas_mesh`,
`rw_mpas_convert`, `rw_wrfbatch`); the Python layer orchestrates,
validates and writes provenance. There is no fallback plotter and no
Python weather-field rendering: if the renderer is absent, the render
door refuses by name.
chunks.title: 3.2 The doors

chunks.text:
## 3.3 Why the dycore is pinned and the physics is refereed by observations

Two different correctness standards apply to the two halves of the model,
and the difference is the most important thing in this manual.

**The dynamical core is pinned.** The dynamics (the fluid-motion numerics)
is a port of MPAS-Atmosphere v8.4.1, and it is held byte-identical to the
native source's arithmetic as its correctness anchor, kernel by kernel, with
pinned source-line citations. Byte-identity is achievable there, it was
achieved, and every change to the executing modules is guarded by SHA-256
pins so it cannot drift silently. When this manual says "deterministic," it
is backed by dual runs compared byte for byte.

**The physics is not MPAS's, so agreement with MPAS is not its standard.**
woof hex runs the WOOF engine's physics suite through a pinned seam.
Whole-model agreement with native MPAS stopped being reachable the moment
that choice was made, so physics parity with MPAS is **retired as a goal**,
and the physics is judged by **skill against observations** (MRMS
precipitation and radar products, ASOS surface stations). Matching another
model's choices was never evidence of being right; matching the atmosphere
is.

**A declared divergence** is the stated-in-full form of a known difference: measured
magnitude, named mechanism, named observational referee. There are three
([`docs/declared-divergences.md`](../declared-divergences.md) is the
register; the README quantifies them).

**Every magnitude below is measured against native MPAS-A, and it carries a
tense.** The three entered the repository already finished on 2026-08-20 with
no receipt directory, no card and no run commit; the commit that introduced
them pinned engine `629ddb6f0`, which is the ceiling on when they were taken.
Three engine pin moves have landed since. The last one is measured to change
nothing on one case (a byte A/B of the two pins found the atmosphere
fingerprint identical at all 31 steps)
but the two earlier moves have no such arm and no magnitude has been
re-measured over 24 h, so whether any of them moved is **NOT MEASURED**.
Read them as pre-2026-08-20 numbers.
chunks.title: 3.3 Why the dycore is pinned and the physics is refereed by observations (1)

chunks.text:
1. **Upper-level warm drift**: above level 45 the port warms at +0.019 K/h
   relative to native, one-signed, +0.46 K at 24 h. Fine at 24 h;
   disqualifying for long-range work. Referee: a vertical-profile referee
   (radiosondes or a pinned analysis), MRMS/ASOS cannot see it.
2. **Convective-to-explicit precipitation repartition**: the port's
   Grell-Freitas convection is WRF v4.6.1's 2018 generation, native's is
   the 2013 ensemble fork; about a third less convective rain, roughly half
   made up by explicit microphysics, net domain-mean precipitation about
   **15 % dry against native MPAS-A**. Referee: hourly precipitation,
   declared as MRMS, run against Stage-IV, because the shipped MRMS door
   decodes reflectivity only. **The referee ran and disagreed in sign.**
   Against Stage-IV over CONUS on 2026-08-25 the port is wet in all four
   cases (+0.0247 mm/h paired, 19 in 20 [+0.0041, +0.0606]) and rains over too
   much area (frequency bias at 1 mm/h 1.59 / 1.35 / 1.38 / 0.77). The
   15 % figure belongs to the referee retired on 2026-08-20; the obs sample
   is four cases and is not a skill assessment. Both, with their limits,
   are in the register.
3. **Downstream condensate surplus**: +50 % cloud water, +62 % rain water
   in the domain mean by 24 h, heavier point extrema; a consequence of (2).
   Referee: MRMS reflectivity and the precipitation extreme tail.

None of the three is softened by declaring it. Two of them have now been
judged: the obs-referee ran for the first time on 2026-08-25, four cases
scored against Stage-IV precipitation, MRMS reflectivity and ASOS surface
reports ([`docs/obs-referee.md`](../obs-referee.md)). (2) is scored
against real rainfall. (3) is scored on **both** halves: its
precipitation-extreme half from that run, and its reflectivity half from the
default history stream, which publishes `refl10cm` computed inside the due
step's own WSM6 call. On the one case re-run with the field
(`gfs-20260812-divergence`, 2026-08-25, 720/720 steps) the object referee
counted **86 model 35 dBZ objects against 54 observed**, 8 matched at a median
**110.9 km** displacement: an object surplus pointing the same way as the
declared condensate surplus, on one case. Point CSI is **0.0916** at 20 dBZ
and **0.0097** at 40 dBZ over 643,419 pairs; both pay the documented cost of
comparing a 22 km model box against a 0.01° pixel and should not be read
alone. The other three cases' bundles predate the field and re-run
mechanically.
The cloud-water/rain-water partition itself stays outside MRMS and ASOS scope,
and (1) stays outside what these instruments can see at all. A bias that is wrong against observations is still
wrong: declaring MPAS no longer the referee changes the referee, it does not
clear the finding. Every run receipt and every history file carries
`gf_native_parity_claim: false` beside `gf_declared_divergence` so the
declaration travels with the data.
chunks.title: 3.3 Why the dycore is pinned and the physics is refereed by observations (2)

chunks.text:
## 3.4 What a refusal is

A refusal is the model or a door **declining to publish a result it does not
trust**, before that result can be mistaken for a good one. Refusals are the
product's central safety behavior, and they follow two laws:

- **A refusal names the concrete breakage it prevents.** Not "invalid
  input", the actual consequence: *"the intermediate file has 34 distinct
  first-guess levels but --nfglevels declares 5; declare at least 34."*
- **A refusal names its remedy.** Every doctor gap prints the command that
  closes it. Every missing-engine refusal prints the build line and the
  variable to set. A remedy is only offered when it can actually deliver:
  a remedy that succeeds while the door still refuses is worse than none.

This extends into the integration itself: if a step fails validation (for
example vertical velocity past 200 m/s at some level) the run refuses to
publish that step and stops, rather than writing a frame it does not trust.
A case has been seen to stop early this way (README, *Limitations*). The
forecast driver's `--stop-on-refusal` writes the receipt for the frames
already committed instead of aborting with no receipt; no validation is
relaxed. Chapter 8 is organized around refusals for exactly this reason:
the refusal text is the product's own index into its remedies.
chunks.title: 3.4 What a refusal is

chunks.text:
## 3.5 Receipts

Every door writes down what it did and what it claims: the init door's
`*.provenance.json` (SHA-256 of every input, the engine, the argv, the
output), the render door's `render-manifest.json` (engine digests, per-frame
results, exact invocations), the forecast's `cuda-v841-forecast-receipt.json`
(the claim, and at equal prominence the non-claims and dropped guarantees).
Every number this manual quotes was measured, and the text says on what
and when; a number without that is a definition, not a measurement.
chunks.title: 3.5 Receipts

chunks.text: # 4. Meshes and static fields
chunks.title: 4. Meshes and static fields

chunks.text:
## 4.1 The registered meshes

The port runs **registered** meshes: each entry in the registry
(`src/hexcore/drivers/mpas_mesh_binding.py`) declares the mesh's shape, its file digests,
and its admitted timestep, and a forecast binds the named mesh against the
real files before anything touches the GPU. An unregistered mesh, a wrong
name, or a swapped file is refused by name: the registry runner's
`--selftest` proves all three refusal directions on demand.

The registry holds **21 rows** at this release: the two published NCAR
meshes, one generated uniform global mesh, twelve generated graded
(variable-resolution) global meshes, and six limited-area culls. Between
them they declare five timesteps (120, 100, 75, 60 and 20 s) each admitted
against its own file's `dcEdge`. There is no `--list` flag; a wrong `--mesh`
name prints the whole set, which is how you read it. The registry ships in
the package (`woof/hex/drivers/mpas_mesh_binding.py`), so this works from an
install:

```sh
woof hex forecast --mesh nope --grid x --static y --init z --out out
```

```
woof hex: --mesh 'nope' is not a registered mesh.  Registered meshes are
conus-x1.2971, r4.75.11020, r4.75.14050, r4.75.15755, r4.75.4440, r4.75.7975,
u96.64002, v15.150.38857, v15.60.224197, v15.60.224210, v16.66.195629,
v16.66.195630, v20.80.151649, v4.75.121182, v4.75.123423, v4.75.128019,
v6.75.112676, v6.75.114257, v6.75.120989, x1.40962, x4.163842.  A row pins its
grid and static by byte count and SHA-256 and declares the timestep its real
dcEdge admits; running an unregistered mesh would run an unproved shape at an
unadmitted timestep.  Register the row in src/hexcore/drivers/mpas_mesh_binding.py before
running it.
```

The rows this manual works from, and what each one is for:

| mesh | cells | spacing | dt | provenance of the static | forecast status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `x1.40962` | 40,962 | ~120 km uniform | 120 s | native `init_atmosphere` v8.2.0 (NCAR-published) | proven green (this manual's quickstart ran it) |
| `x4.163842` | 163,842 | 92→25 km variable | 120 s | native `init_atmosphere` v8.4.1 | proven green; the byte-identity anchor case |
| `u96.64002` | 64,002 | ~96 km uniform | 120 s | generated: `rw_mpas_mesh` GP(80,0) + unified `rw_mpas_static` | proven green, the first generated mesh to complete a full-physics forecast |
| `v20.80.151649` | 151,649 | 20 km in 80 km graded | 120 s | generated: hierarchical Goldberg ladder + unified `rw_mpas_static` | proven green, 6 h full physics; regenerates bit-identical to its registered bytes |
| `v16.66.195629` | 195,629 | 16.5 km in 66 km graded | 100 s | as above | proven green, 36/36 steps at 100 s, the finest graded mesh to complete a forecast |
| `v15.60.224210` | 224,210 | 15 km in 60 km graded | 75 s | as above | the largest mesh here; admitted on device memory through the real door, no forecast run |
| `v15.150.38857` | 38,857 | 15-km box in ~136 km | 60 s | generated by the unified writer `rw_mpas_static` | **refused at bind**: collapsed dual edges, see 4.5; its 60 s also holds no anchor |

Three admissions run at bind, all geometry-bound and all before CUDA
allocation. A fourth check, separate from geometry, asks whether the row's
declared timestep holds an EARNED anchor: `woof.hex.dt_admission` carries
five, and a row declaring anything else is refused by name (chapter 6).
chunks.title: 4.1 The registered meshes (1)

chunks.text:
**Timestep admission** checks the declared `dt` against the static file's own
complete `dcEdge` array (`dt <= 0.90 * min(dcEdge) / 125 m/s` for the outer
step; `src/hexcore/timestep_admission.py`). An unsafe declaration is
refused with the actual minimum edge length, the requested dt, the computed
bound, and the remedy: it is never silently reduced. The quickstart's bind
line shows the gate working:
`min(dcEdge)=97076.508 m; dt=120.000 s; limit=698.951 s`.

**Dual-edge admission** checks `min(dvEdge/dcEdge)` against a floor of 0.02
(`src/hexcore/dual_edge_admission.py`). The TRiSK tangential operators
divide by `dvEdge` (`pv_apvm_v841_f32` forms
`grad_pv_tangential = Δpv / dvEdge`) so a mesh with a collapsed Voronoi
edge amplifies a tangential gradient by `dcEdge/dvEdge` and blows up inside
the first outer step no matter what timestep is declared. The floor is one
number for every row with no per-row override, sitting between the roughest
published reading (`x4.163842` at 0.033650) and the measured generated-mesh
dislocation class. Bind prints the reading, here for `u96.64002`:
`min(dvEdge/dcEdge)=0.394671 at edge 6 (dvEdge=32955.613 m), TRiSK
tangential amplification 2.534x; floor 0.02`.

**Cell-coordination admission** checks that no cell carries fewer than five
edges (`src/hexcore/cell_coordination_admission.py`) and records the whole
histogram either way. A Goldberg polyhedron has pentagons and hexagons; a
four-sided cell is a generator defect that no closure invariant detects, and
one of them killed a forecast with a ~197 K standing error at model top.
The floor is one-sided on purpose, only coordination below five refuses,
because an 8-coordinated cell was measured NOT to misbehave and a gate with
no measured breakage behind it is not a gate (4.5).
chunks.title: 4.1 The registered meshes (2)

chunks.text:
## 4.2 Validate a pair: `woof hex mesh-check`

Run this before anything expensive touches a mesh:

```sh
woof hex mesh-check --grid assets/x1.40962.grid.nc --static assets/x1.40962.static.nc
```

It prints a JSON receipt, dimensions, connectivity indexing, and the
SHA-256 of both files (chapter 2 shows the output), and refuses a
defective or mismatched pair by name. The digests it prints are what the
registry pins, so `mesh-check` is also how you confirm your copy of a
registered mesh is the registered bytes.

A regional (limited-area) cull carrying the `bdyMaskCell/Edge/Vertex`
triple is validated against the regional contract (sentinel-tolerant
connectivity keyed to the seven boundary rings, Euler characteristic 1 for
a disk, and the mask-derivation rules) and the receipt gains a `regional`
block: zone width, per-ring cell counts, and the `bdy_mask_sha256` a
regional registry row pins. A culled grid exists before its static does,
so `mesh-check --grid-only --grid <file>` validates the grid alone; the
receipt records `static: null` and any `--static` is not read in that
mode.
chunks.title: 4.2 Validate a pair: `woof hex mesh-check

chunks.text:
## 4.3 Generate a mesh and its static: `woof mesh`

New meshes come from the **engine's** door, `woof mesh`: it generates an
icosahedral Goldberg grid at the resolution you ask for and builds the
matching static in the same run, with no native toolchain anywhere in the
loop. (This door was not present on the published woof 2.5.2 wheel; it
arrives with the 2.5.3 bundle, well below the floor this distribution's
declared `woof>=2.8.0,<2.9` range requires. The commands below were proven from a `woof` checkout.)

**See what a card can hold:**

```sh
woof mesh --list-cards
```

```
cards in <woof>/data/mpas/mesh-sizing.json
  rtx-3080       NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 (10 GiB)
                 NOT MEASURED -- NOT MEASURED. No full-physics footprint run has been made on this part.
  rtx-5070-ti    NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti
                 15,881 MiB (addressable); 70 SM x 1536 threads
                 model 5,384 MiB fixed (2,896 derived store + 2,488 measured residue) + 86,630 B/cell; holds 127,051 cells
                 anchor x1.40962: 40,962 cells measured at 8,768.0 MiB
  rtx-5090       NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
                 32,607 MiB (nvidia-smi total, NOT MEASURED through CUDA); 170 SM x 1536 threads
                 model 9,798 MiB fixed (7,032 derived store + 2,766 measured residue) + 86,630 B/cell; holds 276,081 cells
                 anchor generated: 38,857 cells measured at 13,165.0 MiB
                 anchor x1.40962: 40,962 cells measured at 13,182.0 MiB
                 anchor x4.163842: 163,842 cells measured at 23,334.0 MiB

smoothness bound (provisional): refuse above 3.06 %/cell, published reference 1.53 %/cell
```

**Those rows are the ENGINE's own sizing table, not the port's admission
model, and the two must not be averaged.** They are a line in cell count
(`fixed + slope × cells`) whose anchors predate the port's frame cut; the
port's gate has a different shape and different numbers (4.6). Use this
table to size a mesh at `woof mesh` and 4.6's model to decide whether the
result will run.

**Size a request without writing anything:**

```sh
woof mesh --refine 39.1,-84.5,800,25 --background-km 92 --card rtx-5070-ti --dry-run
```

This asks for a 25-km circle of radius 800 km centered at 39.1N, 84.5W in a
92-km background (the same refinement ratio as the published `x4` family)
sized to fill an RTX 5070 Ti. The dry run prices it at 127,051 cells with a
1.65 %/cell steepest spacing gradient and applies both gates (device budget
and mesh smoothness) before you spend a minute of compute.

Ask for something too steep and the door refuses with the mechanism and the
remedy: this run was kept because the refusal is the door working:

```sh
woof mesh --refine 39.1,-84.5,300,15 --background-km 120 --card rtx-5070-ti --dry-run
```

```
woof mesh: REFUSED: the requested mesh is 4.32 %/cell at its steepest spacing
gradient, past the 3.06 %/cell this release will emit.
  what breaks: A mesh whose cell size jumps faster than the numerics were designed
  for degrades the C-grid gradient and divergence operators across the transition
  band: the errors show up as a standing wave parked on the refinement boundary,
  which looks like weather and is not.
  what to change: widen the transition (a fifth field on --refine, in km), coarsen
  the refinement, or refine a smaller area.  --allow-rough-mesh emits it anyway and
  is reported as a workaround.
```
chunks.title: 4.3 Generate a mesh and its static: `woof mesh

chunks.text:
### A `--spec` request has its own door: `woof hex mesh-plan`

`woof mesh --refine` applies its own smoothness gate at `--dry-run`, shown
above. A `--spec` JSON handed straight to `rw_mpas_mesh --dry-run` does not
get that: the generator sizes the request, prints a receipt and exits 0
without applying either gate its own build applies. Two designs measured
2026-08-28 on the current engine:

* a 0.75/6/75 km design sized clean and the build refused it 87 ms later on
  the transition-band gate: arithmetic on the same steepest-gradient
  number the dry-run receipt had just printed;
* a 0.75/3/15/75 km design sized clean, cleared that gate, relaxed 220,468
  cells for **711 s** and was then refused on the 200 m shortest-dual-edge
  floor, with no grid written.

`woof hex mesh-plan` closes the first and names the second, in about a
fifth of a second:

```sh
woof hex mesh-plan --spec my-case.json --card rtx-5070-ti
```

#### Where that gradient is measured (changed 2026-08-29)

The transition-band gate is arithmetic on one number, and until 2026-08-29
the generator sampled that number on a lattice spread evenly over the whole
globe. At the 50,000 points it used, those sit about 101 km apart, so a
refinement transition narrower than that was stepped over entirely and the
receipt reported the flat background the lattice happened to land on. On an
eight-rung 51.2 km to 200 m ladder it printed 12.12 %/cell for a field that
reads 37.04, and the build admitted a design its own gate exists to refuse.
Nothing in the reading said so, because a maximum over points that missed the
ramp looks exactly like a gentle ramp.

The generator now probes where a spec says its regions are (a shell a few
transition widths wide around each region boundary, resolved across the ramp
rather than along it) and prints two more fields beside the number:
`gradient_probe_points`, what the reading cost, and
`gradient_probe_coverage`, which reads `complete` when every locus where the
field varies was covered. `woof hex` refuses to judge a spec on a receipt
that does not say `complete`, including a receipt from an older engine that
does not say anything, because a number that is not a measurement is not
something to gate on.

Two consequences worth stating plainly. Specs with ramps hundreds of
kilometres wide (every swath the threat metrics emit, and the two examples
above) do not move: the old lattice already resolved them, and their
readings shift in the fourth decimal. Specs with sub-kilometre cores and
short ramps do move, sharply, and some designs that used to build now refuse
before anything is seeded. That is the gate working, not a new restriction:
the band was always that narrow.

And what still is not measured this way: `predicted_cells` and
`region_attainment` on the same receipt are still integrals over the global
lattice, with the resolution limit that implies. Only the gradient follows
the regions.
chunks.title: A `--spec` request has its own door: `woof hex mesh-plan (1)

chunks.text:
It prices the spec through the generator's own sizing integral, applies the
transition-band gate here (so a spec the build would refuse is refused
before the build, with the ramp widening that clears it quoted in the spec's
own units), and prints the shortest-dual-edge floor as what it is: a gate
that reads the finished tessellation, cannot be decided from a spec, and is
predicted (never refused) from the generator's own 0.04 surgery flag
floor. A finest spacing under 5 km is where that prediction turns against
you. `--json` prints the whole receipt; `--out` writes it beside your case.

**Generate for real**: grid and static in one command. The proving run
built a small uniform demonstration pair (a resolution spec plus an explicit
cell count) in under three minutes end to end, the static half in 94.5 s
with its 82 variables:

```sh
woof mesh --out demo.grid.nc --background-km 480 --cells 2562 \
    --name manual-demo --geog <WPS_GEOG-root> --receipt demo.receipt.json
```

```
woof mesh: WROTE demo.static.nc 4908228 82 ea7cf7b3cf57...
woof mesh: wrote demo.static.nc (4,908,228 B, 82 variables, SHA-256 ea7cf7b3cf57...)
woof mesh: nominalMinDc 480,000.000000 m declared as FP32 0x48ea6000 -- the mesh
registry compares this scalar bit for bit
woof mesh: the pair is demo.grid.nc + demo.static.nc
```

A mesh needs both a **resolution** (`--background-km`, `--refine` rows, or
a `--spec` JSON) and a **size** (`--card NAME` to fill a card, or
`--cells N`); giving only one produces a named refusal pointing at the
other. The static lands beside the grid (`--static-out` to move it);
`--no-static` is a workaround, reported as one, because a lone grid file is
refused by the registry before any dycore sees it.
chunks.title: A `--spec` request has its own door: `woof hex mesh-plan (2)

chunks.text:
## 4.4 The geographical data the static is built from

The static builder samples a WPS-GEOG archive (terrain, land use, soil,
green-ness, albedo). The engine stages it:

```sh
woof fetch-geog --root <WPS_GEOG-root> --list     # what is staged / what would download
```

```
  staged  topo_gmted2010_30s: ... (~1798 MiB unpacked)
  staged  modis_landuse_20class_30s_with_lakes: ...
  staged  soilgrids: soilgrids.tar.bz2 824.1 MiB (~12530 MiB unpacked)
fetch-geog: total 2.01 GiB download, ~27.7 GiB unpacked
```

Drop `--list` to actually stage (the proving box's root was staged by this
command; `--datasets mesh` limits the set to what `woof mesh` needs). The
soilgrids archive is ~13 GiB unpacked and only the mesh door reads it.

**A known layout trap, stated so you do not lose an afternoon to it:**
`woof fetch-geog` stages the soilgrids datasets *nested*
(`WPS_GEOG/soilgrids/soilcomp`, `WPS_GEOG/soilgrids/texture_layer1`, …)
while `rw_mpas_static` resolves them *flat* (`WPS_GEOG/soilcomp`, …). On a
tree fetch-geog itself staged, the static build refuses naming five missing
datasets. The working layout on the proving machine bridges the gap with
directory junctions (symlinks on Linux) from the root to the nested copies:

```
WPS_GEOG/soilcomp        -> WPS_GEOG/soilgrids/soilcomp
WPS_GEOG/texture_layer1  -> WPS_GEOG/soilgrids/texture_layer1
...and texture_layer2..4, texture_top, texture_bot
```

This disagreement is a recorded cross-tool defect awaiting an engine-side
fix; until then the bridge above is the supported layout.
chunks.title: 4.4 The geographical data the static is built from

chunks.text:
## 4.5 What a generated mesh is good for today: the exact boundary

**A uniform generated mesh forecasts.** `u96.64002` is ours end to end (grid
from `rw_mpas_mesh`, static from `rw_mpas_static`, init from `woof hex init`
with no native binary at any stage) and it completed a full-physics
forecast on an RTX 5070 Ti at `rc 0`, `status "passed"`, with
`finite: true` in every step's health record.

**A graded generated mesh forecasts too.** A graded global mesh comes from
a JSON spec, a background spacing plus any number of refinement regions
(cap, lat/lon box, polygon), at any ratio, at any coordinates, with no code
path per spec. The mechanism is a hierarchical Goldberg ladder: level 0 is
the same icosahedral subdivision the uniform arm uses, each level halves the
spacing by count-targeted midpoint insertion, and the transition annuli are
drained by count-changing defect surgery. All three of the campaign's graded
spec rows regenerate clean, and `v20.80.151649` regenerates BIT-IDENTICAL to
its registered bytes, every cell centre, ring and edge length exactly equal,
so its completed 6 h full-physics forecast describes what the generator
emits today. Measured across ten
level runs and four generated meshes (3,374 to 224,210 cells),
`min(dvEdge/dcEdge)` lands between 0.0406 and 0.1023: two to five times the
admission floor, zero edges under 0.04 on any of them.

**Two real generator defects had to be fixed to get there, and both are
worth recognising.**

*A four-sided cell.* A Goldberg polyhedron has pentagons and hexagons and
nothing else. The defect surgery's insertion operator placed its new
generator on a near-cocircular quad's own circumcentre, where the new cell's
Delaunay ring is exactly the four quad cells, so it emitted a
QUADRILATERAL, then pinned it during the local polish. Nothing downstream
saw it, because a four-sided cell plus the two heptagons the same operation
makes leaves `sum(6 - nEdgesOnCell)` at exactly 12: Euler characteristic,
degree sum and sphere closure all read correct on an illegal mesh. One such
cell kills a forecast. `v16.66.195630` carries exactly one (cell 195615) and
the model's theta maximum parks on it at the top model level with a ~197 K
standing error, converged in the timestep: dead at step 23 of 36 at 100 s,
step 31 of 48 at 75 s, the same model time. `cell_coordination_admission`
refuses coordination below five at bind and stays, because the mesh it
refuses is still registered and still on disk; `v16.66.195629` is that same
spec row regenerated by the fixed generator, and it runs 36 of 36.

*A polygon region that refined the far side of the planet.* The engine's
polygon containment test accepted on `|winding| > pi`, which cannot tell a
point inside a ring on a sphere from a point whose ANTIPODE is inside it, so
every polygon refinement region refined a congruent ghost of itself on the
opposite hemisphere. The ghost's edge is a step and not a ramp, so the
spacing field fell from the region's spacing to the background across one
cell and the smoothness gate then refused every emitted spec. Fixing the
containment test cleared both symptoms.
chunks.title: 4.5 What a generated mesh is good for today: the exact boundary (1)

chunks.text:
**What is still refused, and why it is not gradedness.** `v15.150.38857`
came from the retired density-biased Fibonacci seed, which is
polycrystalline: it carries 3,447 heptagons beside 3,459 pentagons, and a
pentagon-heptagon quad is near-cocircular, so the Voronoi edge between its
two nearly-coincident vertices collapses, 6.51 m against a 38,658.7 m
`dcEdge`. That is the whole of the old step-0 `FloatingPointError`. The
TRiSK tangential terms divide by `dvEdge`, so the potential-vorticity
gradient across that one edge is amplified 5,935x; a per-launch probe puts
every runaway magnitude in the first outer step on it, and the first
non-finite value in the run is `exner` at a neighbouring cell. No timestep
is a lever against it. That seed is retired to a control instrument, but the
row it produced is the bytes that measured the cost, so it stays registered
and stays refused: the generator refuses to emit such a mesh and the bind
refuses to run one, each naming the measurement.
chunks.title: 4.5 What a generated mesh is good for today: the exact boundary (2)

chunks.text:
## 4.6 Capacity planning by card

**The footprint is not a line in cell count, and you cannot size a mesh with
a pocket calculator.** It has this shape:

```
peak = core(your card, your configuration)
     + Grell-Freitas workspace at min(cells, SMs x 4 x 64) columns
     + YSU workspace        at min(cells, SMs x 16 x 32) columns
     + bytes per cell x cells
```

The two workspace terms grow with your mesh until it is bigger than what
your card can hold in flight, and then they stop. On a 170 SM part those
knees are at **43,520 cells** and **87,040 cells**. Below them the marginal
cost of a cell is higher than the slope; above them it is the slope. A third
term, the RRTMG shortwave column chunk, is sized from the card's resident
threads and never grows with the mesh at all: 1,745.6 MiB on a 170 SM part,
872.8 MiB on a 68 or 70 SM part.

Measured anchors on an RTX 5090 (170 SM) at the merged tip: `x1.40962` (40,962 cells)
peaked at **8,874 MiB**; `x4.163842` (163,842 cells) at **20,446 MiB**. The
shaped row reproduces both exactly.

To size a mesh for a budget, ask the surface: it inverts the model by
bisection because there is no single slope to divide by:

```python
from woof.hex.device_admission import KNOWN_CARDS, model_for_card
model = model_for_card(KNOWN_CARDS["10gib-68sm"])       # or your own CardProfile
model.max_cells(int(9_097 * 1024**2))                   # 68440 cells admitted
model.required_bytes(40_962)                            # 6884963136 free bytes
```

**Ask the question in the configuration you mean to run.** `model_for_card`
takes the configuration second, and it defaults to `"global"`; a limited-area
question must say so or it is answered with the wrong core:

```python
cull = model_for_card(KNOWN_CARDS["10gib-68sm"], "limited-area")
cull.required_bytes(11_020)                             # 6979108286
cull.measured                                           # False -- DERIVED, labelled
```

This is not only a planning surface: it IS the admission gate. The forecast
door, `--preflight` and the driver's own floor all answer from it, and the
door reads your card's multiprocessor count at the moment of the decision
rather than assuming a 5090.

**The margin is not a flat number either.** It is your card's shortwave
workspace plus 11.2 MiB of instrument convention, and each part names what
it absorbs: `ShapedFootprintModel.margin_terms()`. It replaced a flat
512 MiB that named nothing and was measured 1,104 MiB short on a
limited-area cull.

**A limited-area run is a different configuration and carries its own core**,
because the regional device stack builds a padded atmosphere, two levels of
lateral-boundary state and 22 more kernels. At cull cell counts it is about
85 % mesh-independent, which is why a line in cell count over-predicted every
measured cull by 1.2-1.9 GiB. That core is currently an ENVELOPE over five
whole-device samples, not a per-allocation fit, and it over-predicts the
smallest cull by about 1.3 GiB.

**Graded meshes cost nothing extra.** Measured at the model's own protocol,
`v20.80.151649` (151,649 cells) comes in 0.22 % *under* prediction and its
per-allocation census is the uniform mesh's scaled by cell count. The
earlier instruction to size graded meshes with extra margin was installed for
a defect that does not exist and is retired.
chunks.title: 4.6 Capacity planning by card (1)

chunks.text:
- **12 GiB card**: DERIVED, NOT MEASURED, no 12 GiB card exists in the
  measurement fleet, and the answer moves with the card's SM count, so ask
  `model_for_card` with your own profile rather than reading a number off
  this page.  Quoted on the 170 SM measured row (the most conservative,
  because its core and its margin are the largest measured) a full
  12,288 MiB budget carries **57,433 cells**, and the published `x1.40962`
  global mesh needs 10,631 MiB of it (8,874 MiB predicted peak plus that
  card's 1,756.8 MiB margin).  A row derived for a smaller part is
  materially larger: an 84 SM card takes 89,472 cells at the same budget.
- **16 GiB card**: the quickstart's runs on an RTX 5070 Ti (this manual's
  proving card) integrated `x1.40962` full-physics with room to spare.
  That card has its own measured row and the door selects it from the
  card's own multiprocessor count, with no flag: a smaller part is no
  longer priced with a 5090's core.  `--device-fixed-mib` /
  `--device-bytes-per-cell` still exist for a card whose own
  `tools/device_memory_ledger/` run has been made, but they are an escape
  hatch now rather than the remedy of first resort.
- **32 GiB card**: `x4.163842` measured 20,446 MiB at the merged tip and
  admits at **about 21.7 GiB free** (that peak plus the card's own named
  margin, not a flat headroom) so in practice it remains a 32 GiB-card
  configuration: a 24 GiB part running a desktop rarely offers that.  At
  the free memory an idle RTX 5090 actually offered (31,642.6 MiB, measured
  2026-08-26) the shaped model
  carries **266,328 cells**, and the largest mesh this project has
  generated (224,210) admits with room.  Whether such a mesh RUNS is a
  separate question the same preflight answers, and the timestep is no
  longer one number: `woof.hex.dt_admission` holds five earned anchors
  (120, 100, 75, 20 and 5 s) keyed by the CONFIGURATION, the timestep
  together with the cumulus selection.  Rule of thumb `dt ≈ 6 × dx(km)`;
  `v16.66.195629` (16.5 km core) binds and steps at 100 s (chapter 6).

`woof mesh --card NAME` applies its own per-card measured table (the
`--list-cards` output above, with per-card anchors) when sizing a new mesh,
and `--vram-gib X` substitutes a budget for a shared card. The sizing table
and the footprint model above are two separate measurement sets: the
sizing table's anchors predate the current engine pin and are the more
conservative of the two; do not average them together.
